reviews.review:
Glow Ball - The billiard puzzle game takes the basic physics of billiards and turns them into a relaxed puzzle experience built around angles, collisions, positioning, and careful observation. Instead of trying to reproduce a traditional game of pool with conventional rules and competitive matches, it uses billiard-style interactions as the foundation for individual challenges. The result is a small and focused game that feels closer to a physics puzzler than a sports simulation. It was developed and published by WTFOMGames, with the overall design clearly centered on accessibility and experimentation rather than complicated mechanics.

The gameplay is easy to understand but can require more thought than its simple appearance initially suggests. Players must consider the direction of a shot, the point of impact, and how balls are likely to behave after colliding with one another or elements of the environment. Much of the satisfaction comes from studying a situation before committing to an action. Successfully predicting a sequence of movements can be rewarding, particularly when one well-planned shot produces exactly the intended result. The billiards influence makes the basic rules intuitive while still leaving room for puzzle arrangements that would never appear on an ordinary pool table.

Its stages are important to keeping the concept interesting. Different layouts encourage players to reconsider familiar techniques and experiment with alternative approaches rather than simply repeating the same shot patterns. Some situations are straightforward exercises in trajectory, while others place greater emphasis on anticipating several movements ahead. This creates a pleasant mixture of logical planning and experimentation. Not every attempt will succeed as expected, since physics-based games naturally introduce situations where a slight difference in angle can significantly alter the result, but discovering the correct approach is part of the appeal.

Glow Ball also distinguishes itself through its presentation. Dynamic lighting and glowing visual elements give the environments an abstract appearance that fits the puzzle-focused structure. The game does not need realistic pool halls or elaborate scenery because its visual priority is keeping attention on the objects and their movement. The luminous style provides enough personality to prevent the environments from feeling like purely functional test chambers. Its colorful and somewhat surreal presentation works particularly well alongside the slower rhythm of play.

The soundtrack contributes to that relaxed character. This is not a game built around frantic competition, strict tournament pressure, or constant action. Its atmosphere encourages players to take their time, examine the level, calculate a possible solution, and watch the outcome unfold. That meditative quality can make it suitable for shorter sessions when a player wants something uncomplicated yet mentally engaging. At the same time, anyone who prefers fast-paced puzzle games may find the deliberate tempo somewhat subdued.

The greatest limitation is the narrowness of the central concept. Almost everything revolves around variations of billiard-ball physics, so long-term enjoyment depends heavily on whether calculating trajectories and experimenting with collisions remains satisfying to the individual player. There is no expectation of the extensive rule sets, competitive modes, career systems, or multiplayer depth associated with dedicated billiards simulations. This is fundamentally a single-player puzzle game using billiards as its mechanical inspiration. Players specifically searching for realistic pool competition should therefore look elsewhere.

There can also be an element of trial and error. Visualizing the correct angle is one thing, but reproducing the necessary shot within a physics simulation can occasionally require several attempts. For some players, repeatedly refining a trajectory will be an enjoyable part of solving the puzzle. For others, situations where the intended solution appears clear but execution remains slightly inconsistent may become frustrating. Fortunately, the generally calm presentation prevents failure from feeling excessively punishing, and the game is better enjoyed as an experimental experience rather than something that demands perfect performance at every moment.

Steam Deck compatibility is not officially rated by Valve for this title, so there is no Verified or Playable badge that guarantees the handheld experience. Given the game's relatively modest technical requirements and straightforward design, it may still be possible to run it through Steam Deck's compatibility environment, but this should be considered unofficial compatibility. Players may encounter interface, control, display, or Proton-related issues and should not assume complete functionality without testing it themselves.

Overall, Glow Ball - The billiard puzzle game succeeds most when treated as a modest physics puzzler rather than a full billiards package. Its approachable mechanics, abstract glowing presentation, atmospheric audio, unusual level arrangements, and leisurely pacing create a distinctive identity from a very simple foundation. The experience is unlikely to satisfy players looking for substantial progression or realistic competitive pool, but it has a certain charm for anyone who enjoys experimenting with geometry and watching a carefully calculated chain of collisions unfold.

It is a pleasant and accessible physics puzzle game with a relaxing personality and an interesting interpretation of billiards. Its limited scope prevents it from developing into something particularly deep, but the combination of thoughtful trajectories, varied puzzle layouts, atmospheric presentation, and straightforward mechanics makes it worthwhile for players attracted to casual spatial challenges.

Rating: 5/10
